result: A novel Dst-b mutant mouse model was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 to introduce a nonsense mutation in a Dst-b-specific exon. The mutation resulted in truncated Dst-b protein in heart and skeletal muscle, with approximately 50% reduction in Dst-b mRNA in cardiac tissue, while Dst-a expression remained unchanged in brain. Dst isoform 1 mRNA was specifically reduced, while isoforms 2 and 3 were unaffected.
evaluation: Claims C35-C48 provide comprehensive molecular characterization of the Dst-b mutant model. Western blot (C38), qPCR (C40-C43), and RNA-seq data (C44-C46) consistently demonstrate isoform-specific disruption of Dst-b without affecting Dst-a. The data show appropriate controls, statistical analysis, and multiple independent validation methods.

result: Dst-b mutant mice lack the neurological phenotypes characteristic of dt mice. Unlike DstGt/Gt mice, Dst-bE2610Ter/E2610Ter mice showed normal posture, normal muscle spindles, no neurofilament accumulation, normal parvalbumin-positive neurons, and normal motor coordination. Body weight was normal until 1 year of age, after which it became lower than WT mice.
evaluation: Claims C49-C62 demonstrate through multiple behavioral and histological assays that Dst-b mutation does not cause neurological phenotypes. The comparison with DstGt/Gt mice (which lack both Dst-a and Dst-b) provides strong evidence that Dst-a deficiency, not Dst-b deficiency, causes dt phenotypes. Statistical analysis and appropriate controls support the conclusion.

result: Dst-b mutant mice develop late-onset skeletal myopathy characterized by centrally nucleated fibers (CNFs), small-caliber muscle fibers, and fibrosis in soleus, gastrocnemius, and erector spinae muscles at 16-23 months of age. These pathological features were rare at 3-4 months of age. Cardiac fibrosis was also observed in aged mutant mice but not in young mice.
evaluation: Claims C63-C72 document progressive muscle pathology with appropriate temporal controls (young vs. aged mice). Quantitative histological analysis (C66) shows statistically significant increases in CNFs across multiple muscle groups. The age-dependent progression (C65, C72) supports the late-onset nature of the disease. Morphometric analysis (C68) and fibrosis quantification (C69-C71) provide robust evidence.

result: Dst-b mutant mice develop late-onset cardiomyopathy with upregulation of heart failure markers (Nppa, Nppb) and profibrotic cytokines (Tgfb2, Ctgf). ECG analysis revealed prolonged QT intervals and premature ventricular contractions in aged mutant mice, indicating cardiac conduction disturbances. These abnormalities were not present in young mice.
evaluation: Claims C73-C85 provide comprehensive cardiac characterization using in situ hybridization (C73-C75), qPCR (C76-C77), and ECG measurements (C79-C82). The data show statistically significant changes with appropriate age-matched controls. The correlation between severe cardiac fibrosis and PVCs (C83) strengthens the findings. The absence of abnormalities in young mice (C78, C84) confirms late-onset progression.

result: Dst-b mutant mice exhibit protein aggregation in striated muscles characteristic of myofibrillar myopathy (MFM). Desmin aggregates were found in subsarcolemmal regions of skeletal muscle and cardiomyocytes at 16-23 months. These aggregates contained αB-crystallin, plectin, myotilin, and truncated Dst-b proteins. Z-disk displacement was observed in fibers with desmin aggregates.
evaluation: Claims C89-C107 demonstrate protein aggregation pathology through immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence. Multiple proteins characteristic of MFM are shown to co-aggregate (C96, C98, C101, C102). The temporal progression (C95) and subcellular localization data (C90, C93-C94, C105-C106) are well-documented. The conclusion that these aggregates resemble MFM (C107) is supported by comparison with established MFM characteristics (C86-C88).

result: Mitochondrial abnormalities occur in Dst-b mutant muscles, including subsarcolemmal accumulation of mitochondria co-localizing with desmin aggregates and phosphorylated PERK. Expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes (Ndufb8, Sdha, Cox4i1) was significantly reduced, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction. Mitochondrial accumulation was observed at 3-4 months before appearance of desmin aggregates, suggesting it may precede protein aggregation.
evaluation: Claims C109-C117 document mitochondrial pathology through immunohistochemistry (C109-C111) and qPCR analysis (C112-C113). The co-localization with desmin aggregates (C110) and presence of stress markers (C111) support mitochondrial dysfunction. The temporal analysis (C116-C117) suggesting mitochondrial changes precede protein aggregation is intriguing, though the inference (C117) requires caution as it's based on limited time points. Controls for fiber type and oxidative stress (C114-C115) strengthen the specificity of findings.

result: TEM analysis revealed ultrastructural features of MFM in Dst-b mutant muscles, including focal myofibrillar dissolution, Z-disk streaming, subsarcolemmal accumulation of mitochondria and granulofilamentous materials (glycogen granules, disorganized Z-disks, filamentous materials), and dysmorphic nuclei. In cardiomyocytes, nuclear envelope invaginations and crystalline inclusions were observed.
evaluation: Claims C118-C126 provide detailed ultrastructural characterization through TEM. The observations are consistent with established MFM features (C121). The identification of nuclear inclusions in cardiomyocytes (C124-C125) represents a novel finding, though the limited number of reports on similar pathology (C126) makes this particularly noteworthy. The TEM data complement and validate the light microscopy findings.

result: Dst-b mutant cardiomyocytes exhibit unique nuclear pathology including dysmorphic nuclei with deep invaginations and nuclear inclusions containing p62, ubiquitinated proteins, and SUMO proteins. These inclusions were distinct from cytoplasmic aggregates, lacking LC3 and desmin/αB-crystallin. Super-resolution microscopy confirmed co-localization of p62 and ubiquitin within nuclei. The percentage of nuclei with p62-positive structures increased from 0.55% in WT to 14.3% in mutants.
evaluation: Claims C127-C145 document a novel nuclear pathology through multiple imaging modalities (H&E, IHC, TEM, super-resolution microscopy). The quantification (C135) shows statistically significant increase in nuclear inclusions. The molecular characterization (C134, C136, C138) is thorough, and the distinction from cytoplasmic aggregates (C139-C142) is well-established. The use of super-resolution microscopy (C136) provides high-quality evidence for co-localization.

result: RNA-seq analysis of Dst-b mutant hearts identified 728 differentially expressed genes (481 upregulated, 247 downregulated) with FDR<0.1 and p<0.001. Upregulated genes were associated with pro-fibrotic pathways, cytoskeletal regulation, and metabolic control. Downregulated genes were associated with transmembrane ion transport. GO and KEGG pathway analyses confirmed enrichment of muscle-specific terms including dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac muscle contraction.
evaluation: Claims C146-C161 present comprehensive transcriptomic analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<0.1, p<0.001). PCA and hierarchical clustering (C147) demonstrate clear separation between genotypes. The functional enrichment analyses (C156-C160) are consistent with the observed pathology. The inclusion of causative genes for cardiac diseases (C155) strengthens clinical relevance. qPCR validation is mentioned in supplementary data, supporting RNA-seq reliability.

result: Mosaic analysis using conditional DstGt mice demonstrated that myopathy is caused by loss-of-function of Dst-b rather than gain-of-function of truncated protein. Mosaic mice with absent Dst-b protein in heart but variable Dst-a in brain showed cardiac fibrosis, increased Nppa expression, and p62 deposition, similar to Dst-bE2610Ter/E2610Ter mice.
evaluation: Claims C162-C170 address a critical mechanistic question through mosaic analysis. The experimental design (C164) allows discrimination between loss-of-function and gain-of-function mechanisms. Western blot data (C166-C167) confirm the expected protein expression pattern. The observation of similar cardiac pathology in mosaic mice (C168-C169) supports loss-of-function mechanism. However, the mosaic mice also showed mild dt phenotypes (C165), suggesting some Dst-a expression remained, which could complicate interpretation.

result: In silico analysis identified 58 different nonsense mutations (94 alleles) in DST-b-specific exons across worldwide populations (European, Asian, African, American). In Japan, 4 alleles were found among 16,760 alleles, suggesting homozygous/compound heterozygous mutants may exist in ~1 per 16 million people. Two Japanese myopathy patients with compound heterozygous DST variants were identified, though all variants were classified as VUS.
evaluation: Claims C171-C177 present in silico findings and limited patient data. The database screening (C171-C172) is straightforward, but the frequency calculations (C174) assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and may not account for selection against homozygotes. The identification of patients with DST variants (C175) is interesting, but the VUS classification (C176) means pathogenicity is uncertain. The speculation about unidentified familial diseases (C177) is reasonable but requires clinical validation. The lack of functional validation of identified variants limits the strength of conclusions.

result: The study demonstrates that Dst-b isoform is essential for long-term maintenance of striated muscles. Dst-b mutant mice exhibited late-onset protein aggregate myopathy and cardiomyopathy without neuropathy, termed 'dystoninopathy.' The findings suggest that myopathic manifestations in HSAN-VI patients may be caused by DST-b disruption, and that unidentified hereditary myopathies/cardiomyopathies may be caused by DST-b mutations.
evaluation: These claims (C5-C12, C30-C34, C178) represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from multiple experimental approaches. The conclusion that Dst-b is essential for muscle maintenance (C12) is well-supported by the late-onset myopathy phenotype. The suggestion about HSAN-VI patients (C33) is reasonable given the data, though it remains speculative without patient studies. The proposal of unidentified diseases caused by DST-b mutations (C34) is plausible given the in silico findings but requires clinical validation.

result: Background knowledge about DST gene structure, isoforms, and associated diseases. DST encodes three tissue-selective isoforms (DST-a, DST-b, DST-e) and mutations cause HSAN-VI and epidermolysis bullosa simplex. DST-b contains all DST-a-encoding exons, so HSAN-VI mutations could affect both isoforms. Previous dt mouse models had mutations in both Dst-a and Dst-b, making it unclear whether muscle manifestations were cell-autonomous or secondary to neuropathy.
evaluation: Claims C1-C29 present established knowledge from cited literature about DST gene structure, isoforms, and disease associations. These provide appropriate context for the study. The identification of the knowledge gap (C23) - whether muscle manifestations in HSAN-VI are due to DST-b or secondary to DST-a deficiency - clearly motivates the generation of the isoform-specific mutant model.

result: Discussion of MFM characteristics and potential mechanisms. MFM is defined by myofibril disorganization at Z-disks and protein aggregation. The study's findings suggest Dst-b mutations may lead to Z-disk fragility and myofibril disruption. Protein quality control impairment through unfolded protein response, autophagy, and ubiquitin proteasome system may be involved. Heat shock proteins were upregulated in mutant hearts, and p62/ubiquitinated proteins accumulated in muscles.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88, C97, C100, C108, C121, C180-C187 discuss MFM characteristics and propose mechanisms. The comparison to established MFM features is well-supported by cited literature. The mechanistic proposals (C183, C185) are speculative but reasonable given the data. The upregulation of heat shock proteins (C186) and accumulation of autophagy markers (C187) provide some support for these mechanisms, though direct functional studies would be needed for definitive conclusions.

result: Discussion of autophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction in MFM. Autophagy disruption has been reported in dt mice and other MFM models. Mitochondrial dysfunction is recognized in MFM animal models. RNA-seq data suggest mitochondrial dysfunction in Dst-b mutant cardiomyocytes. Altered heart function (long QT, PVCs) may be explained by mitochondrial dysfunction and altered expression of ion transport/muscle contraction genes.
evaluation: Claims C188-C197 discuss autophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction with appropriate citations. The inference about mitochondrial dysfunction from RNA-seq data (C196) is reasonable given the altered expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes. The proposed explanation for cardiac dysfunction (C197) is speculative but plausible. However, direct functional assays of mitochondrial function (e.g., oxygen consumption, ATP production) would strengthen these conclusions.

result: Discussion of nuclear abnormalities and comparison to LINC complex diseases and NIID. Deep nuclear membrane invaginations were observed in Dst-b mutant muscle fibers. Dst-b may be involved in the molecular bridge between LINC complex and cytoskeleton. Nuclear inclusions in Dst-b mutants share molecular features with NIID (p62, ubiquitin, SUMO proteins) but differ from autophagy-deficient mice (lack LC3).
evaluation: Claims C198-C211 discuss nuclear pathology with appropriate comparisons to LINC complex diseases and NIID. The proposal that Dst-b may bridge LINC complex and cytoskeleton (C204) is speculative but supported by cited interaction data (C202) and the observed nuclear pathology. The comparison to NIID (C211) is interesting given the shared molecular components, though the diseases are otherwise distinct. The distinction from autophagy-deficient mice (C206) is well-supported by the LC3 data.

result: Discussion of DST-related diseases and isoform-specific roles. Various genetic diseases are caused by DST mutations. The study suggests unidentified hereditary myopathies/heart diseases may be caused by DST-b-specific mutations. Candidate gene screening of DST-b-specific exons in MFM patients is recommended. Among Dst-b isoforms, Dst-b1 reduction was observed in mutant mice, suggesting its involvement in myopathic phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C212-C227 discuss disease implications and isoform-specific effects. The recommendation for candidate gene screening (C218) is reasonable given the findings. The observation that Dst-b1 is specifically reduced (C225-C226) is interesting and suggests isoform-specific functions, though the functional significance requires further investigation. The speculation about DST isoforms 1 and 2 having different importance in neural vs. muscular tissues (C227) is reasonable but requires validation.

result: Discussion of plakin family proteins and comparison with plectin. Plectin and Dst are both plakin family proteins with overlapping roles in different cell types. Plectin deficiency causes similar pathological alterations to Dst-b deficiency, including desmin aggregation, mitochondrial accumulation, and abnormal nuclear shape. Both proteins localize to similar subcellular compartments and have comparable functions in keratinocytes and Schwann cells.
evaluation: Claims C228-C240 compare Dst and plectin functions with appropriate citations. The comparison is valuable for understanding plakin family protein functions. The observation that some pathological features are shared between Plec-deficient and Dst-b-deficient muscles (C233) supports overlapping functions. However, the differences in severity (e.g., C237) and lethality (C231) suggest non-redundant functions as well. The conclusion about overlapping roles (C240) is well-supported.
